newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul prosecutors question Kim's son over Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: Seoul prosecutors question Kim's son over Hanbo.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors questioned a son of President Kim Young-sam on Friday in connection with a loan scandal that has badly damaged the government's credibility.

A prosecution official said Kim Hyun-chul was questioned over a libel complaint he filed on Tuesday against six opposition politicians who accused him of peddling influence in giving loans to the failed Hanbo Steel Co.
Among the six from the main opposition National Congress for New Politics are party spokesman Chung Dong-young, his deputy Sul Hoon and three other members of parliament.
"The prosecutors will also look into various suspicions raised about Mr Kim Hyun-chul," a prosecution official told Reuters.
Kim Hyun-chul, the president's second son, has said he had nothing to do with $5.8 billion of loans that Hanbo Steel racked up before being declared insolvent on January 23.
Speculation that Kim Hyun-chul maintained close links with Hanbo was fanned by the discovery last week of more than 10,000 copies of a book written by him in a Hanbo Group warehouse in Seoul.
Hanbo Steel is the flagship of the Hanbo Group, South Korea's 14th-biggest conglomerate.

The opposition has said the books found in the warehouse highlighted that Hanbo had been a sponsor of Kim Hyun-chul, the first son of an incumbent South Korean president to be summoned for questioning by prosecutors.
The Hanbo scandal has eaten into the political credibility of President Kim who has sought to project the image of an anti-graft crusader since taking office in 1993.
On Wednesday, prosecutors indicted 10 people, including Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo and three close aides to the president, on bribery and embezzlement charges in the scandal.

Those indicted from President Kim's inner circle are former home affairs minister, Kim Woo-suk, who resigned last week shortly before being arrested for bribery, and lawmakers Hong In-gil and Hwang Byung-tai.
Kim Woo-suk was the third cabinet minister in six months to resign under a cloud of corruption.
As the president's son appeared at the prosecution office for questioning, dozens of angry protesters staged a noisy demonstration demanding a further probe into the scandal.
"Every time a major incident breaks my name is mentioned, but I can no longer remain silent," Kim Hyun-chul said in a recent interview with the Choon-ang Ilbo daily.

Prosecutors said they might also question six opposition politicians who Kim Hyun-chul said defamed him. But apart from them, the prosecution had no plan to summon more political figures in connection with the scandal.
Kwon Roh-kap, a top aide to opposition leader Kim Dae-jung, has also been charged with accepting bribes from the Hanbo founder.
Opposition parties have demanded a new probe, saying prosecutors had only revealed "a few feathers and not the body" of the case.

The National Congress and the United Liberal Democratic Party, which together control 123 seats in the 299-member National Assembly, have called for special legislation to allow independent prosecutors to restart the probe.
They said they would seek a televised hearing during a separate parliamentary probe, for which a special committee had already been formed in the National Assembly.
